description: Defines the five maturity levels used across the Operations Maturity System.

philosophy.title: Artifacts are evidence. Behavior is maturity.
philosophy.explanation: Having an SOP does not mean a process is mature. Having dashboards does not make an organization data-driven. Having a RACI does not mean decision authority is clear. Having recurring meetings does not mean governance exists. Maturity is demonstrated through consistent operating behavior, not through the existence of a document.
examples: Having an SOP does not mean a process is mature.
Having dashboards does not make an organization data-driven.
Having a RACI does not mean decision authority is clear.
Having recurring meetings does not mean governance exists.

levels.name: Reactive
levels.description: People and heroics run the organization. Work happens because specific individuals make it happen, not because the system is designed to produce the outcome.
levels.statement: Ask Sarah. She knows how that works.

levels.name: Repeatable
levels.description: Patterns exist, but execution varies by person, team, and moment. What happens once tends to happen again, informally, but nothing guarantees consistency.
levels.statement: We normally do it this way.

levels.name: Defined
levels.description: Standards, ownership, and processes are established and documented. People can point to how something is supposed to work, and mostly, it works that way.

levels.name: Managed
levels.description: Performance is measured and the operating system is actively governed. Deviations are visible quickly, and there are mechanisms in place to respond to them.

levels.name: Adaptive
levels.description: The operating system continuously learns and improves. The organization doesn't just execute and monitor — it anticipates change and redesigns itself in response.
levels.statement: We know what's changing, why, and what to do next.
